title: Does the sharded duplicate-name check pull further ahead with more targets and threads?
body:
`refuse_repeated_names` in `nail/src/io/records.rs` refuses an input fasta or hmm file that repeats a record name. It hashes every name in parallel, then splits the records into one shard per rayon thread by name hash. Each shard checks its records with its own `HashSet`, so a repeated name lands twice in one shard.

On 2,455,940 mgy targets at 8 threads on the 16-core box, with a warm page cache, the check alone took:

| variant | seconds |
|---|---|
| binary search per record over libsail's name index, one thread | 2.37 to 2.45 |
| the same binary search, 8 threads | 0.23 to 0.24 |
| one `HashSet`, one thread | 0.15 to 0.16 |
| `HashSet` per shard, 8 threads, the one nail uses | 0.04 to 0.05 |

The comment on the shard loop claims the gap should grow with the number of targets and the number of threads. Nobody has measured that. The variants are in `tmp-claude/2026-10-14-serial-overhead/index-split/src/bin/check.rs` on the 16-core box, run as `check <variant> <fasta> <threads>`, with variant one of `bsearch-1`, `bsearch-t`, `hash-1`, `hash-t`.

## Proposal

Run the four variants on the 48-thread box, on several MGnify shards concatenated to well past 2.4M targets, at 8, 16, 32 and 48 threads. If the claim holds, the issue closes with the table. If it does not, the comment changes to match what was measured.

## Open

- Peak memory of the sharded variant, which holds one `HashSet` per shard at once.

notes.author: jackroddy/4125deb5
notes.text:
Measured on the 48-thread box, `catalyst`, at `bb3c392`, pinned to the 48 physical cores of NUMA node 0. The four variants were rebuilt from the descriptions in this issue as `tmp-claude/2026-10-18-serial-overhead-48t/check` on that box. `hash-t` is a copy of `refuse_repeated_names`. The inputs were the 2,455,940-record mgy target file and the first 10,000,000 and 40,000,000 records of `/data/mgnify/fa/mgy_proteins_1.fa`. Every cell is the fastest of 5 runs in one process, or of 3 runs for `bsearch-1`, with the name index built once beforehand and a warm page cache.

Check time in seconds:

| records | threads | bsearch-1 | hash-1 | bsearch-t | hash-t |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2,455,940 | 8 | 3.48 | 0.189 | 0.425 | 0.037 |
| 2,455,940 | 16 | | | 0.213 | 0.034 |
| 2,455,940 | 32 | | | 0.106 | 0.035 |
| 2,455,940 | 48 | | | 0.071 | 0.039 |
| 10,000,000 | 8 | 18.76 | 1.254 | 2.279 | 0.277 |
| 10,000,000 | 16 | | | 1.134 | 0.169 |
| 10,000,000 | 32 | | | 0.563 | 0.137 |
| 10,000,000 | 48 | | | 0.377 | 0.122 |
| 40,000,000 | 8 | 132.4 | 6.22 | 16.01 | 1.236 |
| 40,000,000 | 16 | | | 7.93 | 0.826 |
| 40,000,000 | 32 | | | 3.89 | 0.649 |
| 40,000,000 | 48 | | | 2.59 | 0.467 |

The one-thread variants ran once per size.

The claim in the comment holds in part:

- The lead over `bsearch-t` grows with the number of targets. At 48 threads `hash-t` is 1.8 times faster at 2.4M and 5.5 times faster at 40M.
- The lead over `bsearch-t` shrinks with the number of threads at every size. `bsearch-t` halves its time each time the threads double, and `hash-t` does not. At 2.4M `hash-t` takes about 0.035 s at every count from 8 threads up.
- The lead over `hash-1` grows with threads only from 10M up. At 40M it is 5.0 times at 8 threads and 13.3 times at 48.

`hash-t` is still the fastest variant in every cell. Building the name index, which happens before the check, takes 1.55 s at 2.4M and 28.6 s at 40M. At 48 threads the check costs 2.5% of the index time at 2.4M and 1.6% at 40M.

On the open question of memory: I read the peak RSS from `VmHWM` before and after the timed runs. At 40M, `hash-t` raised it by 1.26 to 1.73 GB, against 0.99 GB for `hash-1`. At 2.4M the figures are 93 to 116 MB against 62 MB. The binary search variants added nothing.

The comment on the shard loop now gives the measured numbers in place of the claim.
